doc.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996

title: Dorsey and Harry James bands and the move to Ellington
summary: Dorsey personnel, a year with Harry James in California, and Tizol telling him Ellington needs a drummer and alto player; James says take me with you.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Yeah, I gave him proper notice this time, yeah. I played it straight this time. And after that, Benny was kind of semi-retired then. He was going to go back to New York and not do too much, so that left an opening for me to join Tommy Dorsey in 1947. And that was a great experience, a wonderful band. He had people in there like Charlie Shavers the great trumpet player, Ziggy Elman was still in the band then, Paul Smith on piano, and Tommy himself was just superb you know. I stayed with him for three years, and then joined Harry James for one year out in California. I wanted to go to California to study with Buddy Baker, who is presently my composition teacher. And the one year with Harry was great. Well in that band they had Willie Smith playing lead alto and Juan Tizol, the great valve trombonist who used to be with Duke. And I stayed at Juan Tizol’s house. So Juan said “I’ve got to talk to you and Willie because I just talked to Duke Ellington today.” I said “really?” He said “yeah.” He said “he’s looking for a lead alto player, Johnny Hodges is leaving, and he’s also looking for a drummer.” So now what do we say to Harry James? So all three of us went to Harry James and we said “Harry—” Of course we had an out with Harry because he wasn’t working every night. He was working like Fridays and Saturdays and that’s about it, just weekends. We said “Harry” all three © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -5-

of us said “we have a chance to join Duke Ellington’s band.” So he looked at us and hesitated for about fifteen seconds, then he said “take me with you.” I’ll never forget those words you know. But he was a great man. Harry was a great player and a sensational band besides you know. But I did get a chance to work with him for a while. And then of course after that, of course with Ellington, there are so many stories about that band, and Ellington himself was an element of surprise, always. Because you never knew exactly what monumental piece of music he was doing for a certain occasion that other bands didn’t do. You know, besides the ballrooms and the theaters and television coming in, we were in on the first Sacred Concert that was done in Grace Cathedral in San Francisco. So just to be a part of that was something. You know I look back at that as really an experience, you know?
